moments.title: From training camp to prison camp
moments.text: Camp Douglas, a Union training camp on the South Side around today's 31st St and Cottage Grove Ave, began holding captured Confederate soldiers. By the war's end an estimated 25,000 to 26,000 prisoners had passed through it.

moments.title: Thousands of deaths
moments.text: Disease, including scurvy, dysentery and smallpox, and exposure to the cold killed thousands of prisoners; some were shot as punishment. A federal record counts 4,039 Confederate dead, and monuments give 6,000.

moments.title: Reburied at Oak Woods
moments.text: The dead, first buried in the City Cemetery on the lakefront, were moved to a mass grave at Oak Woods Cemetery, now called Confederate Mound; sources give 1866 or 1867.

moments.title: The mound is raised
moments.text: Work at Confederate Mound raised the grave and added plaques around its granite monument, which stands about 30 feet tall.

moments.title: Today: a neighborhood over the camp
moments.text: Homes and a park cover the old camp in Bronzeville, where a historical marker tells its story, and archaeologists have dug test pits on the grounds.

facts.label: Prisoners who died
facts.note: The federal count; monuments and some accounts say as many as 6,000.

checked.notes: Location near 31st and Cottage Grove; a training camp that held prisoners 1862 to 1865 (NPS, Clio, monument inscription). Deaths: a U.S. government record gives 4,039; monuments and CBS say up to 6,000, so the story now says 'at least 4,000', with 6,000 as the high estimate. Prisoners 25,000 to 26,000 by source. Reinterment at Oak Woods dated 1866 (VA) or 1867 (federal report); mound raised and plaques added 1911.
